description:
Team ORYSEL - Polytechnic University of Chiapas, IT2ID Engineering

Challenge: CLPS - Lunar Mission Browser

Mission: Intuitive tool to visualize Sun and Earth position from lunar south pole to evaluate power and communication windows for planners, educators and public.

Specializations: Backend & API, Frontend, UX/UI, Scientific Communication and Project Management.
summary:
Choosing where to land on the Moon comes down to two questions: will the lander get sunlight for power, and will it see Earth for a direct radio link? Near the south pole, where Artemis is headed, a few degrees of terrain can take away both. Today, answering this for one site means stitching together ephemeris tables, illumination maps and custom scripts.

MOON DIAL answers it in one place. For any coordinate on the Moon, it computes hour by hour where the Sun and Earth sit in the local sky, using NASA's SPICE toolkit and the DE440 ephemerides, and turns that into power windows, communication windows, the longest night, the longest radio blackout and a GO / NO-GO verdict. A new point takes about two seconds; sites can be compared side by side, and a launch delay can be tested before it happens. The same verified numbers are shown for specialists, the public, educators and kids.

Every result was checked against NASA JPL Horizons: across 5,768 comparisons, the largest difference is 0.000027°. All data is open NASA data, and every coordinate cites its source.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

A lunar lander needs two things to survive: sunlight for power and a direct line of sight to Earth for communication. MOON DIAL tells mission planners, educators and students, for any landing site, when both are available, for how long, and what the worst gaps look like.

For each site it reports:

- Sunlight, Earth visibility and the time both are available at once (% of the period).

- The longest night, which sizes batteries and survival heaters.

- The longest stretch without Earth in view, which drives operations and relay needs.

- Every sunrise, sunset, earthrise and earthset, timed to the second.

- A viability score and a GO / NO-GO verdict, with the reasons behind it.

Example: at the IM-2 site (Mons Mouton, south pole), the Sun is up 59% of the month, but Earth is in view only 73% of it, with a 7.8-day stretch without Earth and a 12.2-day night. At Reiner Gamma, on the near side, Earth never sets.

WHY IT IS USEFUL

1. One answer instead of several tools. Today a planner combines Horizons tables, illumination maps and custom scripts for every candidate site. MOON DIAL joins power and communication into one view.

2. Any point, on demand. Users are not limited to a catalog: they type a latitude and longitude, and the server computes a new site with SPICE in about two seconds.

3. Launch slips. Missions rarely leave on the planned day. The Compare view shifts the landing date and shows how each site's windows change.

4. Blind-spot detection. A site that loses both the Sun and Earth is flagged before effort is spent on it. Our Shackleton test case, with assumed 10-12° crater walls, drops to 0% sunlight and 0% Earth: NO-GO.

5. One engine, four audiences. Specialist, general, educator and kids views all read the same verified numbers, so the tool used for planning is the same one used in a classroom.

WHAT IS NEW

- Power and direct-to-Earth communication are evaluated together, as one combined window, for any coordinate.

- Mission-grade ephemerides (SPICE + DE440) run on demand behind a simple web interface, instead of being reserved for specialists who can script them.

- Accuracy is measured and shown inside the app, not just claimed.

- Honesty by design: every coordinate carries its source, and every model assumption is labeled as an assumption.

HOW IT WORKS

- Ephemeris engine in TypeScript using timecraftjs (NASA-AMMOS, CSPICE compiled for the web) with NAIF kernels: DE440 planetary ephemeris, the lunar orientation model (moon_pa_de440), leap seconds and planetary constants.

- For each site, it computes the apparent elevation and azimuth of the Sun and Earth every hour for 30 days in the MOON_ME frame, with light-time and aberration corrections, on a 1,737.4 km lunar sphere. Each crossing of the horizon is then refined by bisection to 1 second.

- Web app: React + TypeScript (Vite), responsive from 360 px phones to desktop, in English and Spanish.

- Backend: FastAPI and PostgreSQL on AWS EC2, behind HTTPS (Caddy + Let's Encrypt). Accounts are required; passwords are hashed with scrypt and sessions expire after 7 days.

VALIDATION AND LIMITS

- We compared our engine against NASA JPL Horizons for 4 sites, every hour for 30 days: 5,768 comparisons, with a maximum elevation difference of 0.000027°.

- Current limits: the horizon is smooth (flat terrain) except the Shackleton test case, whose crater walls are assumed. The viability score and environment factors are our own model, not NASA values; what is measured is the position of the Sun and Earth.

NEXT STEPS

- Real terrain horizons from NASA's LOLA laser altimeter, so crater walls and ridges are measured instead of assumed.

- Relay-satellite coverage (for sites without Earth in view) and export of windows for mission timelines.

- Classroom activity guides built on the educator and kids views.

USE OF AI

We used an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) to help write code and documentation, under the team's direction; the team reviewed and tested the results. The 30-second demo video was assembled with AI help from real screen captures of the app and is labeled "AI-assisted edit". No result, coordinate or data value in the app was generated by AI: all of them come from NASA data and the SPICE computation.
